title: Etsy is cracking down on AI slop listings
content:
Etsy is announcing stricter rules about how AI can be used in listings to reduce the volume of AI slop on the platform. In a post, the company says that “many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content” and that sellers are “concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways,” spurring the new policies and restrictions.
Etsy is cracking down on AI slop listings
Etsy’s new AI policies, among other changes, require that a listing’s first photo is unedited.
Under the new policies, every listing must include “at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background,” and all photos must “accurately represent the item a buyer will receive.” The photos that aren’t the first one can be edited with software or AI-powered tools, as long as “the final result remains an accurate representation of the physical product.” The company shared a few examples to demonstrate the type of misleading images that are prohibited, including the cat stuffed animal at the top of this post.
While uploading images for a listing, if Etsy detects that any may be AI-generated, the platform will show a pop-up where you can note if an image was made with AI or not, as shown in a video. If a buyer reports that what they receive is “materially different” from a listing, a seller may be responsible for a refund.
For sellers who offer “functional guides,” which include patterns, recipes, or instructions,” Etsy says that the information in those products “must be your own work, not generated by AI.” Sellers will have to show an “actual result” made from a guide. The company also says that listings made by bots are no longer allowed.
Selling AI-generated art is still allowed on the platform, but a seller must disclose that it was made with AI, Etsy says.

report.summary: Etsy will require unedited first photos, AI disclosure, and ban bot-created listings to curb misleading AI slop.
report.background: Generative AI tools have made it cheap and fast to produce realistic product images, patterns, recipes, and even entire listings. On marketplaces like Etsy, which built its brand on handmade and unique goods, that has created a trust problem: buyers cannot always tell whether a photo or product involves AI, and honest sellers worry their work will be compared with misleading AI-generated items. Etsy says buyer confusion and seller concern drove the new rules. The move fits a broader platform trend toward AI disclosure, authenticity checks, and provenance signals. As AI image generation improves, marketplaces face pressure to set clearer expectations without banning AI outright, since some sellers legitimately use AI for art, editing, or workflow support.
key_points: Every Etsy listing must include at least one unedited photo of the real item against a real background. All photos must accurately represent what the buyer will receive. Later photos can be edited or AI-assisted, but the final image still has to be a truthful representation of the physical product.

If Etsy suspects an uploaded image may be AI-generated, it will show a pop-up asking the seller to disclose whether AI was used. If a buyer reports that the received item is materially different from the listing, the seller may have to issue a refund.

For functional guides such as patterns, recipes, or instructions, the content must be the seller’s own work and not AI-generated. Sellers also have to show an actual result made from the guide. Listings created by bots are no longer allowed.

AI-generated art is still permitted on Etsy, but sellers must disclose that AI was used. The policy targets misleading AI slop and fake product photos rather than banning AI-assisted creativity outright.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Etsy’s rules add pressure to build better provenance, watermarking, and disclosure tools, because platforms need practical ways to distinguish AI-assisted content from deceptive listings. For developers, the policy creates demand for image-authenticity checks, metadata standards, and seller workflow tools that preserve original photos and editing history. For regular users, the changes may make Etsy listings more trustworthy, but enforcement will be hard: AI detection is imperfect, and manual review cannot scale easily. Sellers may face more paperwork and refund risk, while buyers get clearer signals about what is real, AI-assisted, or misleading.
report.tools: C2PA / Content Credentials and the open-source c2patool CLI can help attach and inspect provenance metadata for images. AI-image detectors such as Hive and Illuminarty are useful for spot checks but imperfect. Sellers should follow Etsy’s Seller Handbook policy updates and keep original, unedited photos plus process records.
